text: You get an array, points, where each point is x, y, and an integer k. Return the k points closest to the origin, zero, zero, by Euclidean distance. You can return them in any order. The answer is guaranteed to be unique, except for the order.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I pick k points out of n. Every point I return must be at least as close as every point I leave out. And the order of my output doesn't matter. Is that right?

Then the first thing I notice: I don't need the square root. The distance is the square root of x squared plus y squared, and square root only grows when its input grows. So comparing x squared plus y squared gives the exact same order, and I can stay in integers the whole time. Are there any constraints on the input size?
k is at least one and at most the number of points, which is at most ten to the fourth. Each coordinate is between minus ten to the fourth and ten to the fourth.

Good. Then int is safe for the squared distance. The biggest value is at a corner: ten to the eighth plus ten to the eighth, two hundred million, well under the int max of about two point one billion. So no overflow. Let me run through the examples. Example one: one, three and minus two, two, with k of one. Squared distances are ten and eight, so minus two, two is the answer. Example two: three, three; five, minus one; minus two, four, with k of two. Squared distances are eighteen, twenty-six, twenty — the two smallest are eighteen and twenty, so the answer is three, three and minus two, four. Both match.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to sort all points by squared distance and take the first k. That's n log n, and with ten to the fourth points it's honestly fast enough, but it sorts all n points even when I only need a few. This problem reminds me of top-k selection with a bounded heap. I keep a max-heap of size k, ordered by distance. It holds the k closest points seen so far, and its top is the farthest of those k — the gatekeeper. When a new point comes in and the heap gets too big, the farthest one is kicked out. It feels backwards to use a max-heap to find the closest points, but I want quick access to the one I'd throw away next.

Here's the plan. One: compare points by squared distance with less-than, so the farthest point sits on top. Two: for each point, push it, and if the heap holds more than k, pop the farthest. Three: drain the heap into the answer. One thing worth flagging — push first, then pop, and the check is size greater than k, not greater or equal. After the push, the heap briefly has k plus one points, so the new point competes fairly. Greater or equal would pop one too many: minus two, minus two with k of one would return an empty list. There's a trade-off here: sorting is n log n, and quickselect is linear on average, but the heap is n log k with order k memory, and it works on a stream. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The lambda compares squared distances; with less-than, the farthest point sits on top. The loop is push, then pop if too big, and at the end I drain the heap into the answer. One thing worth flagging — with decltype of cmp, I must pass cmp into the constructor. If I just write pq with no argument, it fails to compile in C plus plus seventeen, because a lambda type has no default constructor. C plus plus twenty allows it only for a lambda with an empty capture. My capture-by-reference version still fails there, even though it captures nothing, so an empty capture would be the cleaner choice.

Let's dry-run the code on example two, with k of two. Squared distances are eighteen, twenty-six, twenty. The row that matters is the third push: after pushing minus two, four, the heap has three points, one too many. The top is five, minus one, at twenty-six — the farthest — so it gets popped, leaving twenty and eighteen. The raw output is minus two, four, then three, three — farthest first — which is the same set as expected. Corner cases: k equals n never pops, so every point comes back. Corner points at the max range square to two hundred million, no overflow. A flipped comparator makes a min-heap that pops the closest. And Manhattan distance picks the wrong point when two points tie on it.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is n log k: each point is pushed once, there are exactly n minus k pops in the loop, and each heap operation is log k. The drain adds k more pops, k log k. Space is order k for the heap, plus the output; one small cost is that each push copies a vector of ints. In the worst case, k is close to n, so log k is close to log n and the heap is no better than sorting. With ten to the fourth points, the heap took about a quarter of a millisecond at k of one, but about one point nine milliseconds at k equal to n.
So is a heap the fastest way here?

Honestly, no. If I have all the points up front, nth element is the fastest. It's quickselect, linear time on average, and it moves the k closest points to the front, in no particular order — which is all this problem asks for. In my timing, it took about a quarter of a millisecond, and the heap only beats sorting when k is small; at k of five thousand it's slower than just sorting. The heap's real strength is different: it uses only order k memory, and it works on a stream. If points keep coming in, I can't run quickselect on data I haven't seen yet. Oh, one more thing — the output comes out farthest first. That's fine here, but if someone wanted closest first, I'd just reverse the answer, in linear time in k.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You dropped the square root early and proved int can't overflow, with the real max of two hundred million. You explained why a max-heap finds the closest points, and why it's push then pop with greater than k. And when I asked if the heap is the fastest, you said no — quickselect is linear on average — and named where the heap really wins: small k and streaming data. Good work.
